------------------------------------------------------------------------

R is a data analysis environment. RStudio is a desktop interface to R (sometimes referred to as an integrated development environment-or IDE for short). Unlike most desktop environments you have been exposed to so far, R does not take instructions from a point-and-click environment, its instructions are provided by simple lines of text.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Launching the RStudio software
*
RStudio is available in two forms: a **server-based** application and a **desktop** based application. Some of you may have already used the server-based version of RStudio which is accessed through a web browser. In this course, we will make use of the desktop version of the software (i.e. an installed version of RStudio and R). Note that you can install [R](https://cran.r-project.org/) and [RStudio](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/#rstudio-ide-oss-downloads) on your personal computer if you want to tackle these exercises independent of the computer lab.

To start RStudio on the lab computers, click in the Windows Search field and type "RStudio". When the RStudio application appears in the list of search results, click it to launch the program.

![](img/rstudio.png){width="544"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Setting up the R environment

## Installing packages

This course will make use of four packages: `sf` which is used to load, manipulate and visualize vector files; `terra` which is used to load, manipulate and visualize raster files; `spatstat` which will be used for point pattern analysis; `spdep` which will be used to analyze spatial autocorrelation in the data.

You can install packages in one of two ways: via command line or via the RStudio interface.

### Option 1: Command line

If you choose to install the packages via the command line, type the following lines of code in the console, one line at a time.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
install.packages("sf")
install.packages("spatstat")
install.packages("terra")
install.packages("spdep")
```
:::


### Option 2: RStudio interface

If you choose to install the packages via RStudio's pull-down menu, click on the **Packages \>\> Install** tab and list the packages to be installed in the *Packages* field separated by commas.

![](img/image1.jpg)

> If you are given the option to either compile the packages from source or install the precompiled binaries, choose the **binary installation** option.

## Opening a new R script

If an empty R script is not already open in RStudio, open a new one now.

![](img/image2.jpg)

R scripts are usually saved using the **.R** extension. For this tutorial, you may choose to name the script **r_intro.R**. Be sure to save the script regularly as you add or modify code.

![](img/image4.jpg) 

## Setting an R session's work space

If you plan to read or write files in a specific directory, it is helpful to explicitly define the R session's working directory. To set a session's working directory, go to **Session \>\> Set Working Directory \>\> Choose Directory**. In this example, you will want to set the working directory to the folder that houses the sample dataset.

![](img/image3.jpg){width="409"}

## Loading (activating) packages

Installing a package on your computer is typically a one-time process. However, to use the package in the current R session, you must load it with the `library()` function.

In this exercise, we will load and prep the data for a point pattern analysis using the `spatstat` package. We will therefore not need to load the `spdep` package which won't be used until we tackle spatial autocorrelation in later exercises.

Type the following in the script:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(sf)
library(spatstat)
library(terra)
```
:::


### Running commands from an R script

When you type commands in an R script, the code is not executed automatically. To run a command, place the cursor anywhere on the line and press **Ctrl+Enter** (Windows) or **Cmd+Return** (Mac). RStudio will send that line of code to the *Console* and execute it.

Alternatively, you can click the **Run** button at the top of the script window to execute the current line or selected lines.

Place the cursor on the first line and press **Ctrl+Enter**. Repeat for the remaining lines. The result of the execution will appear in the *Console* pane.

You can also highlight multiple lines of code and press **Ctrl+Enter** to execute all selected lines at once.

> NOTE: You may see warning messages and red text in the Console when loading these packages. In most cases, these messages can be safely ignored.
 
------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Loading GIS data into R

## Loading shapefiles

R can readily read shapefiles, but it does not automatically read all geodatabase formats without additional tools or packages.

First, we will load the Massachusetts polygon shapefile into R and save the contents of that shapefile to an object called `s2`. Note the use of the assignment operator `<-` which *assigns* the output to its right to the object to its left. The name of the shapefile must end with the `*.shp` extension, but note that the function understands that the shapefile consists of *multiple* files.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
s2 <- st_read("MA.shp")
```
:::


> NOTE: if you get the error message `Error: Cannot open "MA.shp"; The file doesn't seem to exist.`, then you probably did not properly set the working directory (see earlier step) or, you have a syntax error in the file name.

R can work with spatial objects in different internal formats (or object classes). For example, `spatstat`'s functions require that specific object classes be used. Throughout this tutorial, we will convert GIS data into several object classes used by `spatstat.` Polygons defining the study area will be stored as `owin` objects, point locations as `ppp` objects, and raster-like surfaces as `im` objects.

The `MA` layer will be used to define the study extent. In `spatstat`, study areas are represented as `owin` objects. We will therefore use the `as.owin` function to convert the `s2` object to an `owin` object.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
w  <- as.owin(s2)
```
:::


The coordinate unit associated with the spatial object inherits the underlying coordinate system's map units--`meters` in this example. Such small units may make it difficult to interpret the output of some operations given that some analyses may generate very small values (i.e. density based analyses) or very large values (i.e. distance based analyses). We will therefore convert the map units from meters to kilometers using the `rescale.owin()` function. Note that 1000 m = 1 km.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
w.km <- rescale.owin(w, 1000)
```
:::


The second parameter in the `rescale.owin()` function, `1000`, tells R to divide the planar unit by 1000.

Next we will load the Walmart stores shapefile (`Walmarts.shp`) using the same functions, but instead of storing the shapefile as a polygon boundary, we will convert the point shapefile to a `ppp` formatted point object.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
s1   <- st_read("Walmarts.shp")  
p    <- as.ppp(s1)  # creates a ppp object
p.km <- rescale.ppp(p, 1000)
```
:::


By default, R will adopt a rectangular extent for the point data.

![](img/image5.jpg){width="220"}

As you will learn in subsequent classes, point patter analyses require an explicitly defined study area. If none is provided, a simple rectangle is assumed as is the current case.

If, however, an explicitly defined study area is desired, the study area should be defined in the point patter. For example, if the State of Massachusetts is to define the study area, then the `Window()` function should be used to assign the `w.km` object created earlier to the `p.km` object.

![](img/image6.jpg){width="220"}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
Window(p.km) <- w.km
```
:::


Note the uppercase `W` in the function `Window()`!

In point pattern analysis, a point's attributes are called **marks**. Since we will be only interested the spatial arrangement of Walmart locations and not in any store characteristics, we remove the marks. Replacing the points' marks with `NULL` removes the attributes.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
marks(p.km) <- NULL
```
:::


## Loading Raster Files

Next, we will load the population density raster file `pop_sqmile.img` using the `rast()` function from the `terra` package, then we'll convert it to an `im` object that is recognized by `spatstat` and name the object `r.km` once re-scaled.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
img  <- rast("pop_sqmile.img") # Load raster file
df   <- as.data.frame(img, xy = TRUE) # Convert to XYZ data table
r    <- as.im(df)             # Convert XYZ table to im object
r.km <- rescale.im(r, 1000)
```
:::


------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Visualizing Spatial Objects

We can plot the raster and overlay it with the point layer. Several plotting options are available including the base `plot` function which will be used in this tutorial. However, there are many R packages that will help improve the "look" of a map including `tmap` and `ggplot2`.

In the following code chunk, we will plot the point data. We'll assign a yellow fill color to the point symbol. The point symbol type is defined by the `pch = 21` parameter.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(p.km, pch = 21, bg = "yellow", main = "Walmart stores")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Getting_started_with_R_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=384}
:::
:::


Point symbol types are defined by a number. The above point symbol is number `21`. Other point symbols available in R are shown below:


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Getting_started_with_R_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=384}
:::
:::


To plot a raster, you can use the `image` function (as well as the `plot` function). Here, we'll adopt a built-in color scheme using the `hcl.colors` function.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
image(r.km, main = "Population density", col = hcl.colors(50, rev = TRUE))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Getting_started_with_R_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=384}
:::
:::


In the following chunk of code, we will plot both the raster and point layers. To add a "layer" to an existing map, include the `add = TRUE` parameter.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
image(r.km, main = "Population density", col = hcl.colors(50, rev = TRUE))
plot(p.km, pch = 16, add = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Getting_started_with_R_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=384}
:::
:::


This wraps up this tutorial.
